newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices firm but traders stay wary of OPEC deal.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices firm but traders stay wary of OPEC deal.

text.p: Oil markets were firmer on Friday after reversing losses made on Thursday when an OPEC deal to freeze output quotas helped to pull prices lower.
Oil traders saw the deal as bearish because they felt the ageing cartel was powerless to stop cash strapped countries like Venezuela and Nigeria quota busting.

The Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) decided to roll over its existing quota ceiling of 25.03 million barrels per day (bpd) despite chronic quota busting which has boosted output to around 27 million bpd in recent months.
OPEC's attempts to put a positive spin on the deal were clumsy and "not a good way to convince the market of a "new dawn" in OPEC attitudes," said Leslie Nicholas of brokers GNI in London.
"It is definitely a question of "we'll believe it when we see it" as far as production cutbacks are concerned," he added.
Despite trader concerns of oversupply, oil prices bounced higher on Friday on the temporary absence of Iraqi oil and short-term tightness of Atlantic basin crudes.
Brent blend crude oil futures, the world benchmark grade, was up 25 cents at $18.10 a barrel at 1353 GMT and well clear of support above a recent 12-month low of $17.32.

Iraq has said it expected to resume exporting oil under a U.N. oil-for-food pact next month. But the temporary absence of Iraqi oil after six-months of oil sales in the first half of the year helped boost prices.
Russian Urals crude, the grade which competes most directly with Iraqi crude, has enjoyed a lift since Iraq stopped selling crude earlier this month.
It has gained about 55 cents a barrel compared to the benchmark Brent crude as refiners used to plentiful Iraqi oil rushed to buy alternative grades.
Under the terms of a United Nations accord implemented last December, Iraq is permitted to sell $2.14 billion worth of oil over 180 days to raise money for food and medicine.
Those sales, quota busting by OPEC and a seasonal decline in oil demand have driven prices down to $18 a barrel from $25 at the start of the year.
Brimming oil tanks are already beginning to weigh on prices for next winter.

In Europe and the United States, winter heating oil stocks are about 20 percent and 13 percent above year ago levels, respectively. And traders say the summer gasoline season in the West stalled at the starting line.
Some traders believe a cold winter and further delays to planned oil production in countries outside of OPEC could stem the losses.
Oil demand in Asia, eastern Europe, Latin America and China is booming and helping to offset more sluggish demand in Western industrialised nations.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) in Paris sees world oil demand putting in a big seasonal jump of 3.2 million bpd in the fourth quarter this year from the current third quarter.
If OPEC does manage to trim output for a couple of months the market "will take notice," said Nicholas.
In addition, the big financial funds who have increasingly traded oil in recent years could be important.
Some dealers believe they are holding big short positions, or bets that prices will fall, in oil, attracted by the 28 percent price slide this year.
If they decide to buy back those positions en masse they would drive prices back towards $20 a barrel, traders said.
